Stage 3 · Grammar

Finished time, or time that is still open?

Two tenses, one question, and the answer is always in the time expression.

Read these four sentences from the recording.
  • I’ve lived in New York for about three years now.
  • When I moved into my flat three years ago, the rent was already quite high.
  • It has gone up three times since then.
  • It took me more than an hour to get to work today.
Why is the last sentence in the past simple, even though today is not finished?
Both forms describe finished events. The difference is the time frame you put around them.

The present perfect and the past simple both refer to something that is over. What separates them is not the event but the period the speaker places it in. The past simple puts the event inside a finished period, cut off from now. The present perfect keeps a live connection to the present moment.

The clearest way to feel this is with a minimal pair. I lived in New York for three years tells your listener that you no longer live there. I’ve lived in New York for three years tells them you still do. The words are almost identical; only the verb form carries that information. This is why choosing wrongly does not just sound foreign — it communicates something you did not mean.

The present perfect is used in four recognisable situations: an unfinished period measured by for or since; a period that has not ended (today, this week, this month); life experience where the time is not the point (Have you ever…?); and a past action whose result matters now (I’ve lost her number). The past simple is used everywhere else, and in particular whenever a finished time is stated.

That last point is absolute and worth fixing now: a stated finished time makes the present perfect impossible, however recent the event. I saw him five minutes ago — not I’ve seen him five minutes ago. This is also why questions with when almost always take the past simple: when is asking for exactly the kind of specific finished time the present perfect cannot accommodate.

Before you look at the table: the table below pairs the two forms against the time expressions that go with each. If you learn nothing else, learn which time words belong in which column — they will decide for you.
The two tenses, side by side

The four small words that decide it
WordMeansExample
forhow long the period isI’ve lived here for three years.
sincewhen the period startedIt has gone up since then.
yetnot up to now — in negatives and questionsI haven’t been mugged yet.
agoa finished point — past simple onlyI moved in three years ago.

The single question. Is the time period over? Yesterday is over, so past simple. This week is not over, so present perfect. The verb follows the time expression, not your feeling about it.

A finished action inside an open period still takes the past simple. It took me an hour to get to work today — the journey ended, even though the day has not.

The mistake to avoid. Never put a finished time with the present perfect: not I have seen it yesterday but I saw it yesterday.

The other mistake. For something that started in the past and continues now, English uses the present perfect, not the present simple: not I live here for three years but I’ve lived here for three years.

Full grammar reference — present perfect simple vs past simple

What it is

Both forms refer to events that are over. The difference is not in the event but in the time frame the speaker puts around it. The past simple places the event in a finished period, cut off from now. The present perfect keeps a connection to the present: the period is still open, the result still matters, or the time is simply not the point.

What it means, and what it does

Compare I lived in New York for three years and I’ve lived in New York for three years. The first says you no longer live there; the second says you still do. Nothing but the verb form carries that information, which is why choosing wrongly does not just sound foreign — it says something you did not mean.

When and why we use it

The present perfect and the past simple both refer to something that is over. What separates them is not the event but the period the speaker places it in. The past simple puts the event inside a finished period, cut off from now. The present perfect keeps a live connection to the present moment.

The clearest way to feel this is with a minimal pair. I lived in New York for three years tells your listener that you no longer live there. I’ve lived in New York for three years tells them you still do. The words are almost identical; only the verb form carries that information. This is why choosing wrongly does not just sound foreign — it communicates something you did not mean.

The present perfect is used in four recognisable situations: an unfinished period measured by for or since; a period that has not ended (today, this week, this month); life experience where the time is not the point (Have you ever…?); and a past action whose result matters now (I’ve lost her number). The past simple is used everywhere else, and in particular whenever a finished time is stated.

That last point is absolute and worth fixing now: a stated finished time makes the present perfect impossible, however recent the event. I saw him five minutes ago — not I’ve seen him five minutes ago. This is also why questions with when almost always take the past simple: when is asking for exactly the kind of specific finished time the present perfect cannot accommodate.

Typical situations

You need this contrast whenever you talk about your life and experience, describe how long you have done something, give news, complain about a situation that is still going on, or tell somebody about a trip, a job or a place you have lived.

  • Finished time — the period is over: yesterday, last night, in 2019, two years ago, when I was a child.I moved into my flat three years ago.
  • A sequence of past events — a story or a report, once the time frame is set.It took me an hour to get to work and nearly as long to get home.
  • Unfinished time up to now — for, since, all my life, so far — the situation continues.I’ve lived in New York for about three years.
  • Inside an unfinished period — today, this week, this month, this year — the period has not ended.Over the past month I’ve been to the theatre three times.
  • Life experience, time not stated — ever, never, before — the point is that it happened, not when.Have you ever been mugged?
  • A present result — the past action explains the situation now.I haven’t been mugged yet, but my best friend has.
  • Recent news — just, already, yet — the event is fresh.I’ve just started salsa classes.

How it differs from similar structures

for + present perfect = still true · for + past simple = finished. I’ve worked here for five years (I still do) vs I worked here for five years (I don’t any more).
ever / never / before pull the present perfect · ago / last / in 2019 / yesterday pull the past simple. If both appear, the finished time wins.

How to build it

Past simple: subject + past form  (regular: verb + -ed)
Present perfect: subject + have / has + past participle
Negative: didn’t + base verb  ·  haven’t / hasn’t + past participle
Question: Did + subject + base verb?  ·  Have / Has + subject + past participle?
Past simple — affirmativeI moved in 2021. · She went last night.
Past simple — negativeI didn’t move. — base form after didn’t.
Past simple — questionDid you move? · When did you move?
Present perfect — affirmativeI have lived here for years. · She’s gone home.
Present perfect — negativeI haven’t seen it yet.
Present perfect — questionHave you seen it? · How long have you lived here?
Short answersYes, I did. / No, I didn’t. / Yes, I have. / No, she hasn’t.
Adverb positionjust, already, never, ever go between have and the participle; yet goes at the end.

Saying it — contractions and stress

  • have and has are weak and contracted in speech (I’ve, she’s, we’ve), which is why learners often cannot hear the present perfect at all in natural English.
  • ’s before a past participle is has, not is: She’s gone = she has gone.
  • In short answers the auxiliary is stressed and never contracted: Yes, I have., never Yes, I’ve.

Usage notes and exceptions

  • A stated finished time makes the present perfect impossible, however recent the event: I saw him five minutes ago, not I’ve seen him five minutes ago.
  • A question with when almost always takes the past simple, because when asks for a specific finished time.
  • The conversation often starts in the present perfect and then moves into the past simple once the time frame is established: Have you been to Almaty? — Yes, I went last spring.
  • This morning can take either form, depending on the time of speaking. At 10 a.m. it is still unfinished (I’ve had two coffees this morning); at 8 p.m. it is over (I had two coffees this morning).
  • American English often uses the past simple with just, already and yet. Both varieties are correct; be consistent within a piece of writing.
  • Been vs gone: She’s been to the theatre (and is back) vs She’s gone to the theatre (still out).

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • I have moved into my flat three years ago. → I moved into my flat three years ago.Ago marks finished time, so the past simple is required.
  • I live here for three years. → I’ve lived here for three years.For with an unfinished period needs the present perfect.
  • When have you seen it? → When did you see it?When asks for a finished time.
  • Did you ever be mugged? → Have you ever been mugged?Ever about life experience takes the present perfect.
  • I didn’t saw the film yet. → I haven’t seen the film yet.Yet takes the present perfect, and didn’t takes the base form.
  • She has went home. → She has gone home.The present perfect needs the past participle, not the past simple form.

More examples in context

  • unfinished periodI’ve lived in New York for about three years now.
  • finished eventThe rent was already high when I moved in.
  • counting up to nowIt has gone up three times since then.
  • experienceI haven’t been mugged yet, but my best friend has.
  • finished detailLuckily she wasn’t hurt — they just took her bag.
  • finished todayIt took me more than an hour to get to work today.
  • inside this monthOver the past month I’ve been to the theatre three times.
  • recent newsI’ve just started salsa classes.
  • negative experienceI’ve never lived anywhere with so much to do.
  • question and answerHave you ever played it? — Yes, I played it last night.

A tip for remembering it

Look for the time expression first — it decides for you. Ago, yesterday, last, in 2019, then → past simple. For, since, ever, never, yet, already, just, so far, this week → present perfect. If there is no time expression at all, ask whether the period is closed. If it is still open, use the perfect.

Before you practise — the key rules

  1. Past simple = a finished period, disconnected from now.
  2. Present perfect = an open period, a life experience, or a result that still matters.
  3. A stated finished time (ago, yesterday, last week) forces the past simple.
  4. For and since with the present perfect mean the situation continues.
  5. When questions take the past simple.
  6. Use the past participle after have / has — not the past simple form.
